_comment: Declarative policy for CROSS-REPO and SELF-REPO workflow dispatch credentials (#149, #359).
The problem this file closes: dispatch used to run on a universal CLASSIC PAT.
On 2026-09-16 that token was observed carrying admin:enterprise, admin:org,
delete_repo, repo, workflow and write:packages. A token that can delete every
repository in the org was sitting in CI so that one workflow could ask another
workflow to start. One leaked job log is the whole org.
The end state: dispatch works, and nothing in CI can delete a repo or touch the org.
Enforced by 9_others/test/test_dispatch_credential_scope.sh, which reads THIS file.
Never extend banned_for_dispatch by editing the tester — edit this list.
_approved_secret_comment: One purpose-named secret, one credential, set on every repo that dispatches.
The NAME did not change in the #149 migration — only the VALUE behind it, from a
universal classic PAT to the fine-grained token described in required_permissions.
Keeping the name stable is what let the migration happen without a flag day:
the workflows already read this name, so rotating the value is a GitHub-UI-only
step with no code change and no window where dispatch is broken.
_banned_comment: Universal / general-purpose credentials that must never appear in a dispatch binding.
CGC_GHCR_PAT is the live one and the reason this list exists: commit 329e41fec added
fallback when the purpose-named secret was missing from this repo. The secret is now
set here (verified 2026-09-16), so the fallback bought nothing and silently widened
the dispatch path back to a classic PAT with delete_repo.
CGC_GHCR_PAT itself is NOT banned repo-wide: it is still the correct credential for
ghcr.io package reads (read:packages), which genuinely requires a classic PAT.
This list is about the DISPATCH path only.

_comment: WHAT THE GUARD IS ALLOWED TO SEE. Before #20/L4 this was a hardcoded list of three
directories scanned at -maxdepth 1 for '*.yml' ONLY. A `curl .../dispatches` or a
`gh workflow run` written inside a .sh was therefore invisible: the banned universal
PAT could come back through a shell script and Phase 50 would stay GREEN. A guard
that cannot see the file cannot fail on it.
So the scan scope is DATA now, like everything else in this file. Three knobs:
file_extensions   — which files can even be read
exclude_dirs      — directory basenames pruned anywhere in the tree
dispatch_markers  — what makes a file a DISPATCHER, i.e. in scope at all
Roots are not listed here on purpose. The scan walks the whole repository plus every
dispatch_consumers[].checkout_paths tree, recursively. A hardcoded root list is the
same blind spot one level up: a dispatch moved into a new directory would silently
stop being checked, and nothing would say so.
_file_extensions_comment: Every file type present in this fleet that can hold an HTTP call or a gh invocation.
yml/yaml — GitHub Actions workflows and Dagu DAGs, the original scope.
sh/bash  — 459 shell scripts here; this is the gap L4 was raised for.
workflows over the REST API from a Node service, so they are real
py       — only 4 files today and none dispatches, but python is the other language
an ops one-liner gets written in, and including it costs one array entry.
WHERE THIS STOPS, and why. Not covered: .nix (372 files — declares packages and
systemd units, never calls the GitHub API), .tf/.hcl (terraform has no dispatch
resource in use here; it provisions VMs), .md (documentation), Makefile (grepped for,
there are none in this repo). If any of those ever gains a dispatch, the fix is to add
the extension to THIS array — never to edit the tester.
_exclude_dirs_comment: Pruned by directory BASENAME, at any depth. z_archive and test-legacy hold retired
code that is never executed — a banned PAT in a file nothing runs is not a live
credential path, and failing on it would push the next person to delete history to
get green. .git and node_modules are not source.
_dispatch_markers_comment: Fixed strings (grep -F), matched anywhere in the file. A file is in scope only if it
SENDS a dispatch. Both forms that exist:
(workflow_dispatch), whether via curl, gh api, or fetch().
gh workflow run  — the gh CLI wrapper for workflow_dispatch, which contains no
'/dispatches' string at all and would otherwise be invisible.
'repository_dispatch' and 'workflow_dispatch' are deliberately NOT markers. Those
strings appear in a workflow's `on:` block, which makes it a RECEIVER, not a sender.
Treating a receiver as a dispatcher would fail cgc-db-index.yml for binding
CGC_GHCR_PAT — which is the CORRECT credential there, for ghcr.io package reads. This
policy bans universal PATs on the DISPATCH path, not repo-wide.
it is in scope (it POSTs /dispatches), it binds CLOUD_INFRA_DISPATCH_TOKEN and nothing
else, and it must stay PASSING. A guard that screams at the one place doing it right

permissions.name: Contents
permissions.why: POST /repos/{owner}/{repo}/dispatches (repository_dispatch) requires Contents: Write. This is what cloud-u-containers uses to tell cloud-infra a container changed.

permissions.name: Actions
permissions.why: Write is required by POST /repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/workflows/{id}/dispatches (workflow_dispatch), used by ship-reconcile.yml to re-queue ship.yml. Read is required by GET .../runs, which the same step uses to VERIFY a run actually appeared.

permissions.name: Metadata
permissions.why: Mandatory baseline permission on every fine-grained token; GitHub selects it automatically and it cannot be removed.

_explicitly_not_granted: Administration — this is what carries repository DELETION on a fine-grained token. Never grant it. Its classic-scope equivalent, delete_repo, is the headline of #359.
Organization permissions of any kind — the classic admin:org equivalent. Dispatch is a repository operation; it has no org-level need.
Packages — the dispatch path never reads or writes ghcr.io. That is CGC_GHCR_PAT's job and stays separate.
Workflows — the ability to EDIT workflow files. Triggering a workflow (Actions) and rewriting one (Workflows) are different powers; dispatch needs only the first.
_residual_risk: Contents: Write on cloud-infra means a leaked dispatch token can push to cloud-infra's default branch.
That is inherent to GitHub's repository_dispatch API — there is no narrower permission that
allows the call. It is bounded to ONE repository and cannot delete it, cannot touch the org,
and cannot reach any other repo. Removing it entirely would mean replacing repository_dispatch
with per-workflow workflow_dispatch (Actions: Write only, no Contents at all), which is a real
option but changes the fan-out: today ONE repository_dispatch fans out to ship.yml,
lint-secrets-coverage.yml at once. Splitting that into six dispatches is exactly the
'silent subset' shape this pipeline has been burned by before. Not taken.

dispatch_consumers._checkout_comment: Where the tester looks for this repo's tree. 'a_solutions' is the path ship.yml already checks cloud-u-containers out to on the runner; '../cloud-u-containers' is the local sibling clone. The repo is PUBLIC, so plain GITHUB_TOKEN can check it out — no dispatch credential is needed to lint the dispatch credential. If NEITHER path resolves the tester FAILS rather than skipping: a cross-repo consumer that silently stops being checked is exactly the blind spot #149 is about.
dispatch_consumers.why: cloud-u-containers is no longer a submodule of cloud-infra (split 2026-09-06). Nothing in cloud-infra watches a push here, so this dispatch is the ONLY signal that a container changed. If it stops firing, every service change sits committed-but-undeployed while the Ship page looks idle.

dispatch_consumers.needs: Actions: Write (dispatch) + Actions: Read (verify) on diegonmarcos/cloud-infra
dispatch_consumers.why: Re-queues a lost deploy (#354). GITHUB_TOKEN cannot do this at all: GitHub suppresses runs triggered by GITHUB_TOKEN to prevent recursion, so the dispatch returns 204 and no run is ever created — a silent no-op that looks exactly like success.

_not_a_dispatch_consumer: CGC_GHCR_PAT -> GH_TOKEN -> anonymous and falls through QUIETLY when none work
(`[ -n "$_tok" ] || return 0`). It looks like a dispatch consumer to a naive grep
for a token fallback chain, and it is a genuine silent-probe, but its target is
ghcr.io manifest reads, not the GitHub dispatch API. It is out of scope for #149
and is left alone deliberately. See the report's 'what is NOT covered' section.
